frames.narration: The client sends one query: 50 posts, each with its author and 20 comments, each comment with its author. The guard walks the query text first: depth 3, estimated 2,100 objects, both under the limits (depth 4, cost 5,000).
Level 0: the executor runs Query.posts once. One query, 50 rows. Now it has 50 parent objects, and each field below will be resolved once per parent.
Naive resolvers, level 1: Post.author runs 50 times and Post.comments runs 50 times. None of them can see the others, so each sends its own SELECT. The database has now answered 101 queries.

Naive, level 2: the 50 posts returned 1,000 comments, and Comment.author runs once for each: 1,000 more single-row queries. Total 1 + 50 + 50 + 1,000 = 1,101 queries; on 10 connections that is about 340 ms of simulated time, mostly round trips.

Same query with DataLoader, level 1. The resolvers no longer query: they call load(key). 50 author keys go to the users loader and 50 post ids to the comments loader. Nothing has been sent to the database yet.

The tick ends, so each loader dispatches once. The 50 author keys hold only 12 different users, so the cache keeps 12 and the batch is WHERE id IN (12 ids). The comments loader sends WHERE post_id IN (50 ids). Two queries, run in parallel.

Level 2: Comment.author asks for 1,000 keys. 972 of them are duplicates or users already in the per-request cache, so the loader sends one query for the remaining 28 ids. Without the cache it would still be one query, but with 1,000 keys in its IN list.
Result: 4 queries and 3 sequential rounds, about 24 ms instead of 1,101 queries and 340 ms, with the identical response. The number of rounds is the depth of the query, no longer N.

Now a hostile client sends the same query 50 times as aliases. Depth is still 3, so a depth limit passes it, but the estimated cost is 105,000 objects. The guard rejects it before any resolver runs: 0 queries, and the loader's cache never sees it.
